IN CONVEX POSITION
LIAM KRUER AND JENSEN KOHLMEYER
ABSTRACT. For every integer 𝑑 ≥ 2, we construct a set 𝑃𝑑 ⊂ R2 in strictly convex position with
𝑁𝑑 := | 𝑃𝑑 | = 2𝑑𝑑 2𝑑𝑑+1
, 𝑢 (𝑃𝑑) ≥ 𝑑
4 𝑁𝑑,
where 𝑢(𝑃) counts unordered pairs of distinct points at distance one. Consequently the maximum number of
unit distances determined by the vertices of a convex 𝑛-gon is not 𝑂 (𝑛), giving a negative answer to Erdős
problem 96. The construction combines a coordinate incidence graph with a two-arc seed near antipodal points.
Selected squared distances have errors of order 𝜀4; exact corrections by rotations have size 𝑂 (𝜀3), while the
strict radial support margin is of order 𝜀2. A radius perturbation separates all subset products of the correction
rotations. The construction, convexity, exact pair count, and negation of the linear bound are formalized in
Lean 4 with mathlib.

The question attributed to Erdős and Moser, recorded as problem 96 in Bloom’s catalogue [ 2], asks whether
𝑈𝑐 (𝑛) = 𝑂 (𝑛). Edelsbrunner and Hajnal [ 3] obtained the lower bound 2𝑛 − 7. Aggarwal [ 1] proved the upper
bound 𝑛 log2 𝑛 + 𝑂 (𝑛), improving the earlier upper bound of Füredi. We prove the following.
Theorem 1.1. For every integer 𝑑 ≥ 2, there is a finite set 𝑃𝑑 ⊂ R2 in strictly convex position such that
| 𝑃𝑑 | = 𝑁𝑑 := 2𝑑 𝑑 2𝑑𝑑+1
, 𝑑𝑁 𝑑 ≤ 4𝑢(𝑃𝑑). (1.1)
Corollary 1.2. For every 𝐶 ∈ R and 𝑛0 ∈ N, there is a set 𝑃 in strictly convex position with | 𝑃| ≥ 𝑛0 and
𝑢(𝑃) > 𝐶 | 𝑃| . In particular, 𝑈𝑐 (𝑛) is not 𝑂 (𝑛).
Proof. Choose an integer 𝑑 ≥ max{ 2, 𝑛0} with 𝑑 > 4𝐶 and apply Theorem 1.1. Since 𝑁𝑑 ≥ 𝑑, its set has
the required size. The inequality 𝑢(𝑃𝑑) ≥ 𝑑𝑁𝑑/4 > 𝐶 𝑁𝑑 gives the conclusion. □
The use of subsets of commuting rotations is adapted from Swanepoel and Valtr [ 6]. Their work also
uses perturbations and mixed derivatives to separate configurations. The additional ingredient here is a finite
incidence seed with a strict radial support margin large enough to preserve every vertex after all the rotations.
The argument needs an arbitrarily small parameter for each fixed 𝑑; no bound uniform in 𝑑 is required.
The proof has three parts. Section 2 gives a general amplification lemma. Sections 3 and 4 construct the
seed and its exact corrections. Section 5 proves that the radii can be perturbed so that no two subset products
coincide. Section 7 describes the checked Lean statement and the correspondence with the proof below.

7. LEAN FORMALIZATION AND REPRODUCIBILITY
The accompanying source project formalizes Theorem 1.1, Corollary 1.2, and the negation of the pre-
cise asymptotic statement in the Formal Conjectures library [ 4]. It uses Lean 4.33.1 and mathlib [ 5] re-
lease v4.33.1, pinned to commit
0df444a360eaa60ab8c11dca51a86af692955474.
All geometric arguments first take place in C, using its ordinary Euclidean norm. The linear isometry
Complex.orthonormalBasisOneI.repr transfers the result to EuclideanSpace over R with index type
Fin 2 .
The file Erdos96/ProblemDefinitions.lean reproduces the four upstream definitions required by
the statement: convex independence of a set, the number of unordered unit-distance pairs, the set of possible
counts at a fixed cardinality, and its supremum. Their defining bodies are unchanged. The upstream open
theorem is not imported. The relevant upstream revision is
b82b08faa9006484021c12005ab41287fb2ffb69.
In particular, the formal convexity predicate is ∀𝑥 ∈ 𝑃, 𝑥 ∉ conv(𝑃 \ { 𝑥}) , and the distance predicate is
equality to one. The use of unordered pairs is verified through Sym2; repeated endpoints cannot satisfy the
unit-distance predicate.
The principal public declarations are:
• Erdos96.plane_counterexample: for each 𝑑 ≥ 2, a finite subset of the literal Euclidean plane
satisfying (1.1);
• Erdos96.large_convex_counterexample: the quantified statement of Corollary 1.2;
• Erdos96.erdos_96_false: ¬( 𝑈𝑐 (𝑛) = 𝑂 (𝑛)) with the upstream supremum definition and the
filter atTop on N;
• Erdos96.erdos_96: the equivalent yes/no statement False ↔ 𝑈𝑐 (𝑛) = 𝑂 (𝑛).
The proof structure follows the manuscript. In a few places the formalization uses an equivalent formula-
tion better suited to the library. A finite embedding of the cells into N supplies the distinct digit exponents.
Continuity on a right neighborhood of zero implements the finitely many small-parameter choices. To prove
Lemma 5.2, a rectangular finite difference isolates a single edge; two applications of one-variable mono-
tonicity, using ( 5.2), make that difference strictly nonzero. For the exponential relation, the proof shrinks
to a neighborhood where phase differences have absolute value less than 𝜋 and uses local injectivity of the
exponential. These arguments prove the required existence statements without numerical certificates.
